strings.title: Adding and Subtracting Like Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: When fractions have the same denominator, you're counting the same-sized pieces: add or subtract the numerators, and use the whole as a landing spot.
strings.keywords: numerator, denominator, same-sized pieces, fifths, sevenths, thirds, whole, mixed number
watchFor: Adding the denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10): ask "Did the pieces change size?"
Not renaming 7/5 as 1 2/5: ask "How many fifths make a whole?"
Subtracting the parts separately in 3 1/5 − 3/5: ask "Can you take 3/5 from 1/5? What could you jump to first?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why don't the denominators change?" Land: the denominator names the size of the pieces, and adding or subtracting doesn't change the size. Jump to the whole number first when you go past it.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 fifths and 1 fifth make 3 fifths. Ask: "What are we counting?" Word choice: say "two fifths plus one fifth". Model: numberline +2/5 +1/5

responses.say: 2 fifths and 1 more fifth is 3 fifths.
responses.tip: The target idea: counting fifths.
Added the denominators. Ask: did the pieces get smaller?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 fifths is a whole. Ask: "What's another name for 5/5?" Model: numberline 3/5 +2/5

responses.say: 3 fifths and 2 fifths is 5 fifths, that's 1 whole.

responses.tip: Ask: is the answer more than 3/5? Is 5/10 more than 3/5?

problems.notes: Look for: 2/5 to make 1, then 2/5 more. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 3/5 +2/5 +2/5

responses.tip: Make a whole, just like tenths.
Both names are right. Ask: which is easier to picture?
Ask: two fractions near 1, is the total less than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 sevenths take away 2 sevenths. Ask: "Is it the same as 6 − 2?" Model: numberline 6/7 -2/7

responses.say: 6 sevenths take away 2 sevenths is 4 sevenths.

responses.tip: Subtracted the denominators too. Ask: what size are the pieces?

problems.notes: Look for: 1 is 5/5, so 5/5 − 2/5; or count up from 2/5 to 1. Ask: "How many fifths is 1?" Model: numberline 2/5 >1

responses.say: 1 is 5 fifths, take away 2 fifths is 3 fifths.

responses.tip: Counting up, like with whole numbers.
Ask: should taking away make the number bigger?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/3 to make 3, then 1/3 more. Ask: "How much does 2 2/3 need to make 3?" Model: numberline 2 2/3 +1/3 +1/3

responses.tip: Not wrong. Ask: how many thirds make a whole? Can you rename it?

problems.notes: Look for: back 1/5 to 3, then 2/5 more to 2 3/5. Ask: "Can you go through the whole number?" Model: numberline 3 1/5 -1/5 -2/5

responses.tip: Through the whole number.
Took 1 from 3 in the numerators. Ask: should the answer be less than 3?

strings.title: Times and Divided by Unit Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Times a unit fraction is groups of that fraction; divided by a unit fraction asks how many of those pieces fit. 3 ÷ 1/4 is 12, because 12 fourths fit in 3.
strings.keywords: unit fraction, groups of, how many fit, halves, thirds, fourths, fifths
watchFor: Thinking division always makes smaller (3 ÷ 1/4 = 3/4): ask "How many fourths fit in 3 wholes?"
Mixing up × 1/2 and ÷ 1/2: ask "Groups of a half, or how many halves fit?"
Losing count on the number line: ask "How many in each whole? How many wholes?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is 4 × 1/2 small but 4 ÷ 1/2 big?" Land: 4 × 1/2 is four halves (2). 4 ÷ 1/2 is how many halves fit in 4 (8). Each whole holds 2 halves, 3 thirds, 4 fourths.

problems.notes: Look for: four halves make 2. Ask: "What is four halves?" Word choice: "4 groups of one half". Model: numberline +1/2 +1/2 +1/2 +1/2

responses.tip: Multiplied the denominator. Ask: count the halves.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 halves in each whole, 4 wholes: 8. Ask: "How many halves fit in 4?" Word choice: "how many halves fit in 4". Model: numberline +1/2x8

responses.say: 2 halves in each whole, 4 wholes: 8 halves.
responses.tip: The target meaning: how many fit. x8 means 8 jumps of 1/2.
Found half of 4. Ask: how many halves fit in 4?

problems.notes: Look for: six thirds is 2. Ask: "How many thirds make a whole?" Model: numberline +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3
Look for: 3 thirds in each whole, so 6. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3 +1/3

responses.say: 3 thirds fit in each whole, 2 wholes: 6.
responses.tip: Same picture as 6 × 1/3. Ask: why?
Multiplied. Ask: how many thirds fit in 2 wholes?

problems.notes: Look for: 4 fourths per whole, 3 wholes. Ask: "How many fourths fit in 3?" Model: numberline +1/4x12

responses.tip: x12 means 12 jumps of 1/4.
Ask: why multiply by 4?
Ask: is 3/4 how many fourths fit in 3?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 fourths, 1 whole and 1 fourth. Ask: "Is it more or less than 1?" Model: numberline +1/4 +1/4 +1/4 +1/4 +1/4

responses.tip: Both 5/4 and 1 1/4 are right.
Divided. Ask: groups of a fourth, or how many fourths fit?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 fifths in each whole, 2 wholes. Ask: "How many fifths fit?" Model: numberline +1/5x10

responses.tip: x10 means 10 jumps of 1/5.

strings.title: Taking Fractions from Whole Numbers
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: To subtract a fraction from a whole number, take it from one of the wholes: 3 − 1/4 is 2 and 3/4. Counting up from the fraction works too.
strings.keywords: whole, take from one whole, mixed number, count up, fourths, thirds, fifths
watchFor: Writing 3 − 1/4 = 3 1/4 or 2 1/4: ask "If you eat a quarter of one of 3 pizzas, how much is left of that pizza?"
Subtracting the denominator: ask "How many fourths are in one whole?"
Losing a whole in 4 − 1 1/3: ask "Take away the 1 first. Then what's left to take?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How does knowing 1 − 1/4 help with 3 − 1/4?" Land: take the fraction from one whole (1 − 1/4 = 3/4) and keep the other wholes. Counting up from the fraction to the next whole works too.

problems.notes: Look for: 4 fourths take away 1 fourth. Ask: "How many fourths in a whole?" Word choice: say "one whole take away one fourth". Model: numberline 1 -1/4

responses.tip: Counting up.

problems.notes: Look for: take 1/4 from one of the wholes. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 3 -1/4

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Added. Ask: should taking away make it bigger?
Ask: if you take a quarter from one whole, how much of that whole is left?

problems.notes: Look for: 1 − 3/4 = 1/4, plus 2 wholes. Ask: "What's the same? What changed?" Model: numberline 3 -3/4

responses.tip: Over and back.

problems.notes: Look for: 1 − 2/3 = 1/3, plus 4 wholes. Ask: "How many thirds make a whole?" Model: numberline 5 -2/3

responses.tip: Kept the 2/3. Ask: 1 whole take away 2/3 leaves what?

problems.notes: Look for: take away 1, then 1/3: 3 − 1/3. Or count up from 1 1/3. Ask: "Which part do you take first?" Model: numberline 4 -1 -1/3

responses.say: 1 1/3 up to 2 is 2/3, then 2 more to 4: 2 2/3.
responses.tip: Counting up.
Took only the 1/3, or only the 1. Ask: did you take away both parts?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 − 2 = 4, then 4 − 3/5. Ask: "Could you count up instead?" Model: numberline 6 -2 -3/5

strings.title: Count Up to Subtract Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Subtract mixed numbers by counting up from the smaller one: to the next whole number, then on. 3 1/4 − 1 3/4 is 1/4 to 2, then 1 1/4 to 3 1/4.
strings.keywords: mixed numbers, count up, next whole number, like denominators, distance
watchFor: Subtracting the fractions backwards (3 1/4 − 1 3/4 = 2 2/4): ask "Can you take 3/4 from 1/4?"
Losing the whole numbers: ask "How far is it from 2 to 3 1/4?"
Not renaming 2/4 as 1/2: ask "Is there another name for 2/4?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does counting up get around the tricky fractions?" Land: jump to the next whole number first, then count the wholes and the pieces. Same as whole numbers.

problems.notes: Look for: 1 3/4 up 1/4 to 2. Ask: "How far is 1 3/4 from 2?" Model: numberline 1 3/4 >2
Look for: 1/4 to 2, then 1 1/4 to 3 1/4. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Word choice: "count up to the next whole". Model: numberline 1 3/4 >2 >3 1/4

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Took 1/4 from 3/4 the wrong way round. Ask: should the answer be less than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/5 to 3, then 1 1/5. Ask: "What's the next whole number?" Model: numberline 2 4/5 >3 >4 1/5
Look for: 1/3 to 4, then 2 1/3. Ask: "Is it the same pattern?" Model: numberline 3 2/3 >4 >6 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: if you take 3 2/3, is there more or less than 3 left?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/6 to 2, then 3 more. Ask: "Is it easier with no fraction in the first number?" Model: numberline 1 5/6 >2 >5
Look for: 3/10 to 2, 1 3/10 to 3 3/10: 1 6/10. Ask: "Can you rename 6/10?" Model: numberline 1 7/10 >2 >3 3/10
Look for: 1/4 to 5, then 2 1/4. Ask: "What do you notice about the answers?" Model: numberline 4 3/4 >5 >7 1/4

strings.title: Adding Mixed Numbers
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Add mixed numbers with the same denominator by making a whole: give the first number enough to reach the next whole number, then add the rest.
strings.keywords: mixed numbers, make a whole, like denominators, rename, improper fraction
watchFor: Writing 4 7/5 and stopping: ask "How many fifths make a whole? Can you rename it?"
Adding the denominators: ask "Did the size of the pieces change?"
Forgetting the whole numbers: ask "Where did the 1 in 1 4/5 go?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did making a whole help?" Land: give the first number enough pieces to reach the next whole number, then add the rest. Same move as 2.6 + 0.7.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/4 makes the whole. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 1 3/4 +1/4
Look for: the last one, plus 1. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline 1 3/4 +1/4 +1
Look for: 2/5 makes 3, then 1 2/5 more. Ask: "What does 2 3/5 need to make 3?" Word choice: "make the next whole". Model: numberline 2 3/5 +2/5 +1 +2/5

responses.tip: The target strategy.
Wholes and parts.
Added the denominators. Ask: did the pieces get smaller?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/3 makes 4, then 2 1/3 more. Ask: "What's the same?" Model: numberline 3 2/3 +1/3 +2 +1/3

responses.tip: True. Ask: how many thirds make a whole? Rename it.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 to 3 5/7, 2/7 to 4, 2/7 more. Ask: "Which order did you add?" Model: numberline 1 5/7 +2 +2/7 +2/7
Look for: 3/10 makes 5, then 3 3/10. Ask: "How is this like 4.7 + 3.6?" Model: numberline 4 7/10 +3/10 +3 +3/10

responses.tip: Decimals connection.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/8 makes 3 (from 7/8), then 1 2/8. Ask: "Can you rename 2/8?" Model: numberline 2 3/8 +1 +5/8 +2/8

strings.title: Fractions and Decimals: Same Moves
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: The same strategies work for fractions and decimals: 6 − 2.75 and 6 − 2 3/4 are the same problem. Count up, make a whole, or take too much and add back.
strings.keywords: fraction, decimal, same value, count up, make a whole, quarters, fifths, tenths
watchFor: Thinking fractions need a completely different method: ask "Is 2 3/4 the same as 2.75?"
Mixing up 0.4 and 1/4: ask "Is 0.4 four tenths or one quarter?"
Getting the decimal answer but not the fraction one: ask "What is 0.25 as a fraction?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why did every pair have the same answer?" Land: 2 3/4 and 2.75 are the same number, so the same moves work. Choose whichever form makes the jumps easier to see.

problems.notes: Look for: 0.25 to 3, then 3. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 2.75 >3 >6
Look for: the same problem. Ask: "What do you notice?" Word choice: "2 3/4 is the same as 2.75". Model: numberline 2 3/4 >3 >6

responses.tip: The target idea.
Ask: is 2 3/4 + 3 3/4 equal to 6?

problems.notes: Look for: 0.25 makes 1, then 0.25 more. Ask: "Is it more than 1?" Model: numberline 0.75 +0.25 +0.25

responses.tip: Ask: is 0.5 the same as 0.50? Add the hundredths again.

problems.notes: Look for: the same as the last one. Ask: "Which decimal is 2/4? 3/4?" Model: numberline 3/4 +1/4 +1/4
Look for: 0.4 to 5, then 5. Ask: "Which way?" Model: numberline 4.6 >5 >10
Look for: 2/5 to 5, then 5. Ask: "Is 4 3/5 the same as 4.6?" Model: numberline 4 3/5 >5 >10
Look for: 1/4 and 3/4 make a whole. Ask: "What's the decimal version?" Model: numberline 3 1/4 +3/4 +1

strings.title: How Many Pieces?
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction asks how many pieces you can cut: 5 ÷ 1/4 is 5 wholes cut into fourths, 4 in each whole.
strings.keywords: how many fit, unit fraction, pieces, cut, divide, fourths, thirds, fifths
watchFor: Thinking division makes smaller (5 ÷ 1/4 = 1 1/4): ask "If you cut 5 pizzas into fourths, how many pieces?"
Multiplying by the fraction instead: ask "Are we finding a fourth of 5, or how many fourths fit?"
Not using the pieces in one whole: ask "How many fourths in one whole?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 1 ÷ 1/4 help with all the others?" Land: count the pieces in one whole (4 fourths), then multiply by the number of wholes.

problems.notes: Context: "Cut 1 sandwich into fourths." Look for: 4 pieces. Ask: "How many fourths in one whole?" Word choice: "how many fourths fit". Model: numberline +1/4 +1/4 +1/4 +1/4
Look for: 4 per whole, 2 wholes. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Model: numberline +1/4x8

responses.tip: x8 means 8 jumps of 1/4.

problems.notes: Look for: 4 × 5. Ask: "Do you need to count them all?" Model: numberline +1/4x20

responses.tip: x20 means 20 jumps of 1/4.
Found a fourth of 5. Ask: how many fourths fit in 5?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 thirds per whole, 3 wholes. Ask: "Same idea with thirds?" Model: numberline +1/3x9

responses.tip: x9 means 9 jumps of 1/3.

problems.notes: Look for: 5 fifths per whole, 4 wholes. Ask: "How does one part help?" Model: numberline +1/5x20

responses.tip: x20 means 20 jumps of 1/5.
Ask: how many fifths fit in 4 wholes?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 halves per whole, 7 wholes. Ask: "What's the pattern?" Model: numberline +1/2x14

responses.tip: x14 means 14 jumps of 1/2.

problems.notes: Look for: 3 per whole, 9 wholes. Ask: "How does one part help?" Model: numberline +1/3x27

responses.tip: x27 means 27 jumps of 1/3.
